questions.question_text:
A raffle drum holds $15$ tickets numbered $1$ to $15$, and one is drawn at random.
Let $X$ be the number drawn.
Find $P(X=11)$.

options.why: Used the value $11$ as the numerator instead of the single favourable ticket.
Divided $1$ by the value $11$ rather than by the number of tickets.
Counted the tickets as the $14$ gaps between $1$ and $15$.

questions.solution_text:
The $15$ tickets are equally likely, so $X$ is uniform over $15$ values.
$P(X=11)=\frac{1}{15}$

questions.question_text:
A booklet has $40$ numbered pages and is opened at a random page.
Let $X$ be the page number.
Find $P(X>33)$.

options.why: Included page $33$, although $X>33$ excludes it.
Stopped counting at page $39$, leaving out the last page.
Counted the pages up to $33$ instead of the pages beyond it.

questions.solution_text:
The favourable pages are $34,\ 35,\ \dots,\ 40$, which is $7$ pages.
$P(X>33)=\frac{7}{40}$

questions.question_text:
The random variable $X$ is uniformly distributed over $\{3,\ 7,\ 10,\ 16\}$.
Find $E(X)$.

options.why: Found the median, the halfway point between $7$ and $10$, instead of the mean.
Added the four values but did not divide by $4$.
Gave the common probability $\frac{1}{n}$ instead of the expected value.

questions.question_text:
The random variable $X$ is uniformly distributed over $\{1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7\}$.
Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.

options.why: Gave $E(X^{2})$ without subtracting $\mu^{2}$.
Gave $\mu^{2}$ instead of the difference $E(X^{2})-\mu^{2}$.
Gave the standard deviation $\sqrt{5}$ rather than the variance.

questions.question_text:
A bag holds four beads marked $1$, $1$, $2$ and $3$.
One bead is drawn at random and $X$ is the number on it.
Is $X$ uniformly distributed?

options.text: No, because $P(X=1)=\frac{1}{2}$ while $P(X=2)$ and $P(X=3)$ are each $\frac{1}{4}$.
Yes, because one bead is drawn from four, so each has probability $\frac{1}{4}$.
options.why: Gave $\frac{1}{n}$ to the four beads instead of to the three distinct values of $X$.

options.text: Yes, because $X$ has three values, so each has probability $\frac{1}{3}$.
options.why: Assumed any finite set of values is uniform without checking the probabilities.

options.text: No, because the values $1$, $2$ and $3$ are not equally spaced.
options.why: Tested the spacing of the values rather than their probabilities, and the values are in fact equally spaced.

questions.solution_text:
Two of the four beads are marked $1$.
$P(X=1)=\frac{2}{4}$
$=\frac{1}{2}$
$P(X=2)=P(X=3)=\frac{1}{4}$
The probabilities are not all equal, so $X$ is not uniformly distributed.

questions.question_text:
Each value of a uniformly distributed random variable has probability $0.025$.
How many values does the variable have?

options.why: Read the digits of $0.025$ as $\frac{1}{25}$ and ignored the decimal place.
Divided $10$ by $0.025$, shifting the decimal point one place too far.
Divided $0.1$ by $0.025$ instead of dividing $1$ by it.

questions.question_text:
Twelve cards numbered $1$ to $12$ are shuffled and one is drawn at random.
Let $X$ be the number on the card.
Find the probability that $X$ is a multiple of $4$.

options.why: Counted only $4$ and $8$, stopping before $12$.
Counted the even numbers instead of the multiples of $4$.
Counted the factors of $12$, namely $1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 6$, instead of its multiples.

questions.solution_text:
Each card has probability $\frac{1}{12}$.
The multiples of $4$ from $1$ to $12$ are $4,\ 8,\ 12$, which is $3$ cards.
$P(X \text{ is a multiple of } 4)=\frac{3}{12}$
$=\frac{1}{4}$

questions.question_text:
The random variable $X$ is uniformly distributed over $\{6,\ 9,\ 12,\ 15,\ 18\}$.
Find $\sigma$, correct to two decimal places.

options.why: Stopped at the variance and did not take the square root.
Took the square root of $E(X^{2})$ without subtracting $\mu^{2}$ first.
Took the square root of the mean instead of the square root of the variance.
